---
title: "Deduplicating documents"
subtitle: "Find repeated records before they distort a collection"
description: "Learn how exact, normalized, and near-duplicate checks behave on Riverton workforce documents."
categories: [documents, deduplication, workforce research]
---

Before training and evaluation, one repeated record can make a collection look
larger than it is. The coordinator sees the same training sentence more than
once and has to decide whether it represents a repeated record or a separate
notice.

That choice affects later counts. Duplicate documents can inflate phrase and
label frequencies. They can also place the same information in both training
and evaluation splits.

This lesson works at the document level. A **duplicate** is a record that the
analyst should not count separately for the research question.

Lesson 12 builds augmented examples with `source_family_id`. Those rows also
need protection against overlap between splits. This page uses a smaller
constructed set to show the distance calculation.

::: {.callout-note}
Riverton is a teaching case. The documents and duplicate families below are
fictional.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

After this lesson, you should be able to:

- explain why duplicate documents change downstream counts.
- find exact duplicates with a SHA-256 hash.
- find formatting-only duplicates with a normalized hash.
- compare near duplicates with character trigram distance.
- choose a threshold by naming the error it makes cheaper.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Build a small comparison set

The comparison starts with the sentence file. The code prepares tables,
normalizes text, and calculates fingerprints and distances. It then compares
pairs and plots thresholds.

A **hash** is a fixed-length fingerprint made from text. The same input gives the
same hash. A different input should give a different hash. Hash comparison
examines exact identity rather than similarity.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(digest)
library(stringdist)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

workforce_sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)

source_text <- workforce_sentences |>
  filter(sentence_id == "s006") |>
  pull(text)

unrelated_text <- workforce_sentences |>
  filter(sentence_id == "s004") |>
  pull(text)

documents <- tibble(
  doc_id = c("D01", "D02", "D03", "D04", "D05", "D06"),
  source = c(
    "Riverton sentence s006",
    "Exact author copy",
    "Formatting author copy",
    "One-word author variant",
    "Near distractor",
    "Unrelated Riverton sentence s004"
  ),
  text = c(
    source_text,
    source_text,
    "  THE employer   pays for certification   TRAINING. ",
    "The employer covers certification training.",
    "The employer pays for certification exam.",
    unrelated_text
  ),
  duplicate_family = c(
    "certification-training",
    "certification-training",
    "certification-training",
    "certification-training",
    "certification-exam",
    "spreadsheet-skills"
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| html-table-processing: none

knitr::kable(
  documents |>
    select(doc_id, source, text),
  col.names = c("Document", "Source", "Text"),
  caption = "Six documents prepared for duplicate comparison",
  format = "html",
  table.attr = 'style="white-space: pre-wrap;"',
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(workforce_sentences), 28L),
  identical(source_text, "The employer pays for certification training."),
  identical(unrelated_text, "Applicants need basic spreadsheet skills."),
  identical(nrow(documents), 6L),
  identical(sum(documents$duplicate_family == "certification-training"), 4L)
)
```

The author wrote this six-row set to demonstrate a known failure mode. Four
rows form one marked duplicate family. They contain the source sentence, an
exact copy, a spacing-and-case copy, and a one-word paraphrase. The exam
sentence changes the claim but retains much of the original wording. The
spreadsheet sentence is unrelated.

## Find exact duplicates

An **exact duplicate** has the same text byte for byte. The code hashes each text
value with SHA-256. In the code, `\(value)` is R shorthand for "for each value,
execute the small calculation that follows."

```{r}
documents <- documents |>
  mutate(
    exact_hash = map_chr(
      text,
      \(value) digest::digest(
        value,
        algo = "sha256",
        serialize = FALSE
      )
    )
  )

exact_groups <- documents |>
  count(exact_hash, name = "documents") |>
  filter(documents > 1L)

exact_duplicate_pairs <- sum(choose(exact_groups$documents, 2))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| html-table-processing: none

knitr::kable(
  documents |>
    transmute(
      doc_id,
      text,
      hash_start = str_sub(exact_hash, 1, 12)
    ),
  col.names = c("Document", "Text", "SHA-256 start"),
  caption = "Exact hashes before normalization",
  format = "html",
  table.attr = 'style="white-space: pre-wrap;"',
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(n_distinct(documents$exact_hash), 5L),
  identical(nrow(exact_groups), 1L),
  identical(exact_groups$documents, 2L),
  identical(exact_duplicate_pairs, 1)
)
```

Only the source and the exact copy match, giving one exact duplicate pair. The
formatting copy receives a different fingerprint because capital letters and
extra spaces are real characters.

## Normalize before hashing

**Normalization** applies a recorded rule before text comparison. This rule
converts text to lowercase and replaces consecutive whitespace with one space.
It removes formatting differences but also removes capitalization and layout
information.

```{r}
documents <- documents |>
  mutate(
    normalized_text = str_squish(str_to_lower(text)),
    normalized_hash = map_chr(
      normalized_text,
      \(value) digest::digest(
        value,
        algo = "sha256",
        serialize = FALSE
      )
    )
  )

normalized_groups <- documents |>
  count(normalized_hash, name = "documents") |>
  filter(documents > 1L)

normalized_duplicate_pairs <- sum(choose(normalized_groups$documents, 2))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  documents |>
    transmute(
      doc_id,
      normalized_text,
      hash_start = str_sub(normalized_hash, 1, 12)
    ),
  col.names = c("Document", "Normalized text", "Normalized SHA-256 start"),
  caption = "Normalized hashes after lowercasing and whitespace squishing",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(n_distinct(documents$normalized_hash), 4L),
  identical(nrow(normalized_groups), 1L),
  identical(normalized_groups$documents, 3L),
  identical(normalized_duplicate_pairs, 3),
  identical(
    documents$normalized_text[1:3],
    rep("the employer pays for certification training.", 3L)
  )
)
```

The normalized hash joins three rows, which make three duplicate pairs. That is
useful here, but risky for a flyer where line breaks or all-capital headings
carry meaning.

## Measure near duplicates

A **near duplicate** is similar enough to require a check even when its
text is not identical. A **character trigram** contains three consecutive
characters. The code extracts every overlapping trigram from each normalized
string. It then removes ordering and duplicate trigrams to form a set.

Jaccard distance is the share of trigrams in the combined sets that do not
appear in both. The distance is 0 for identical sets and 1 for sets with no
shared trigrams. Without order, this measure describes differences in surface
text rather than meaning.

```{r}
comparison_pairs <- expand_grid(
  left_doc = documents$doc_id,
  right_doc = documents$doc_id
) |>
  filter(left_doc < right_doc) |>
  left_join(
    documents |>
      select(
        left_doc = doc_id,
        left_text = text,
        left_norm = normalized_text,
        left_family = duplicate_family
      ),
    by = join_by(left_doc)
  ) |>
  left_join(
    documents |>
      select(
        right_doc = doc_id,
        right_text = text,
        right_norm = normalized_text,
        right_family = duplicate_family
      ),
    by = join_by(right_doc)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    manual_duplicate =
      left_family == right_family &
        left_family == "certification-training",
    jaccard_distance = map2_dbl(
      left_norm,
      right_norm,
      \(left, right) stringdist::stringdist(
        left,
        right,
        method = "jaccard",
        q = 3
      )
    )
  )

calibration_pair <- tibble(
  left_text = "Evening shifts require a valid forklift certification.",
  right_text = "Evening shifts require a valid forklift certificate."
) |>
  mutate(
    jaccard_distance = stringdist::stringdist(
      left_text,
      right_text,
      method = "jaccard",
      q = 3
    )
  )

calibration_distance <- calibration_pair$jaccard_distance
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  comparison_pairs |>
    transmute(
      pair = str_c(left_doc, right_doc, sep = " / "),
      manual_duplicate,
      jaccard_distance = round(jaccard_distance, 4)
    ),
  col.names = c("Pair", "Hand-marked duplicate", "Jaccard distance"),
  caption = "Pairwise distances across the six comparison documents",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  calibration_pair |>
    mutate(jaccard_distance = round(jaccard_distance, 4)),
  col.names = c("Left text", "Right text", "Jaccard distance"),
  caption = "Calibration pair for reading the Jaccard scale",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(comparison_pairs), 15L),
  identical(nrow(calibration_pair), 1L),
  identical(sum(comparison_pairs$manual_duplicate), 6L),
  identical(round(calibration_distance, 4), 0.1132),
  identical(
    comparison_pairs |>
      filter(left_doc == "D01", right_doc == "D04") |>
      pull(jaccard_distance) |>
      round(2),
    0.32
  ),
  identical(
    comparison_pairs |>
      filter(left_doc == "D01", right_doc == "D05") |>
      pull(jaccard_distance) |>
      round(4),
    0.2917
  )
)
```

The calibration strings explain the scale but are separate from the comparison
set. Two sentences that differ only in `certification` versus `certificate`
score 0.1132. In the constructed set, the exam distractor scores 0.2917
against the source. The meaning-preserving paraphrase scores 0.32.

The distractor replaces one short word, while the duplicate replaces a longer
phrase. Surface overlap therefore ranks the changed meaning as more similar.
Real collections can contain such pairs. This small set makes the mechanism
visible.

## Compare thresholds

A **threshold** is the distance at or below which the pipeline joins two
documents. The lesson does not fit the threshold. The team tries several values and
counts both kinds of outcome.

```{r}
threshold_sweep <- tibble(
  threshold = c(0, 0.2, 0.3, 0.35, 0.7, 0.99)
) |>
  mutate(
    caught_true = map_int(
      threshold,
      \(cutoff) sum(
        comparison_pairs$manual_duplicate &
          comparison_pairs$jaccard_distance <= cutoff
      )
    ),
    wrongly_joined = map_int(
      threshold,
      \(cutoff) sum(
        !comparison_pairs$manual_duplicate &
          comparison_pairs$jaccard_distance <= cutoff
      )
    )
  )

perfect_threshold <- threshold_sweep |>
  filter(caught_true == 6L, wrongly_joined == 0L)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  threshold_sweep,
  col.names = c(
    "Threshold",
    "True duplicate pairs found",
    "Distinct pairs wrongly joined"
  ),
  caption = "Near-duplicate results at six threshold values",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(threshold_sweep$caught_true, c(3L, 3L, 3L, 6L, 6L, 6L)),
  identical(threshold_sweep$wrongly_joined, c(0L, 0L, 3L, 3L, 4L, 9L)),
  identical(nrow(perfect_threshold), 0L)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-dedup-threshold
#| fig-cap: "Duplicate pairs found and distinct pairs wrongly joined at each evaluated threshold."
#| fig-alt: "Step chart with two lines across Jaccard distance thresholds from 0 to 0.99. The count of duplicate pairs found remains at 3 until threshold 0.35 and reaches all 6 afterward. The incorrectly joined distinct-pair count increases from 0 to 3 at threshold 0.3, then 4, then 9. No threshold finds 6 duplicates and incorrectly joins 0 distinct pairs."
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the plotting code"

source("R/lesson-figures.R")

sweep_lines <- threshold_sweep |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(caught_true, wrongly_joined),
    names_to = "result",
    values_to = "pairs"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    result = if_else(
      result == "caught_true",
      "true duplicate pairs caught",
      "distinct pairs wrongly joined"
    )
  )

line_colours <- c(
  "true duplicate pairs caught" = lesson_colours[["accent"]],
  "distinct pairs wrongly joined" = lesson_colours[["contrast"]]
)
label_colours <- c(
  "true duplicate pairs caught" = lesson_text_colours[["accent"]],
  "distinct pairs wrongly joined" = lesson_text_colours[["contrast"]]
)

ggplot(sweep_lines, aes(x = threshold, y = pairs, colour = result)) +
  geom_step(aes(linetype = result), linewidth = 0.9, direction = "hv") +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  geom_text(
    data = \(d) filter(d, threshold == max(threshold)),
    aes(label = str_c(pairs, " ", result), colour = I(label_colours[result])),
    hjust = 0,
    nudge_x = 0.02,
    family = lesson_font,
    size = 10,
    size.unit = "pt"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = line_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c(
      "true duplicate pairs caught" = "solid",
      "distinct pairs wrongly joined" = "22"
    ),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = threshold_sweep$threshold,
    guide = guide_axis(n.dodge = 2),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.55))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 9, by = 3)) +
  labs(
    title = "No threshold finds every duplicate without joining distinct pairs",
    subtitle = "Pairs joined at or below each evaluated Jaccard distance threshold",
    x = "Jaccard distance threshold",
    y = "Pairs"
  ) +
  theme_lesson(grid = "y")
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(sweep_lines), 12L),
  setequal(names(line_colours), unique(sweep_lines$result)),
  setequal(names(label_colours), unique(sweep_lines$result)),
  identical(max(sweep_lines$pairs), 9L)
)
```

For this constructed set, 0.2917 is smaller than 0.32. The distractor is closer
to the source than the paraphrase is. Because those two distances are ordered
that way, no threshold on these pairs can match the paraphrase without also
joining the distractor. The comparison shows how a threshold reduces one error
at the cost of another in this set. It does not establish a general law of
deduplication.

## Deduplication at scale

The `expand_grid()` step builds all pairs, with $O(N^2)$ computational
scaling. This approach works for a small teaching set. On large datasets,
all-pairs Jaccard calculations require too much time and memory.

Production systems avoid $O(N^2)$ all-pairs comparisons through Locality
Sensitive Hashing (LSH) and MinHash. These algorithms operate on **shingles**,
overlapping sequences of text units. MinHash summarizes set similarity, while
LSH groups likely near matches for comparison. Packages such as R's
`textreuse` and Python's `datasketch` can group near duplicates across
millions of documents without comparing every pair.

## What to remember

- Duplicate documents can inflate counts and leak between training and evaluation.
- Exact hashes find only byte-for-byte duplicates.
- Normalized hashes find some formatting-only duplicates but remove formatting information.
- Character-trigram Jaccard distance measures surface overlap, not preserved meaning.
- Near-duplicate thresholds change the numbers of missed duplicates and wrongly joined records in this set.
- The right threshold depends on which error costs more for the project.

The system can remove exact duplicates automatically. A person must examine
near matches before any training or evaluation split. These threshold results
describe the constructed set rather than a universal setting for Riverton
documents.
